goal.name: Block fixture (test)

track.name: Block Periodization Program
track.description: Twight's sequential blocks for operator fitness: accumulate volume, convert it to intensity, then realise it. Each block is about a month; the cycle repeats.

phase_sequence.name: Accumulation
phase_sequence.description: A month of high volume at moderate intensity on the six-day week: strength, circuit and accumulation key days, recovery days between them, one long endurance day. Power-endurance and strength-endurance are the targets; maximal strength and speed are not chased.

phase_sequence.name: Transmutation
phase_sequence.description: Volume comes down and intensity goes up, converting the accumulated capacity into usable power-endurance. Progress one lever at a time: less rest on bodyweight work or more load on barbell and kettlebell work — never both at once.
phase_sequence.intensity: Higher; one progression lever at a time

phase_sequence.name: Realization
phase_sequence.description: Low volume at peak intensity, so the qualities built in the previous blocks show up as performance. Recovery days stay in place; the mind is trained alongside the body.

goal.notes: Six-day week: 3 key sessions (strength, circuit, accumulation), 2 recovery sessions, 1 long endurance, 1 full rest. Intensity model is hard/easy alternation — not polarized (no 80/20 split), but structured hard-day/recovery-day cycling. Progression levers are deliberate: reduce rest (bodyweight work) OR increase load (barbell/KB), never both simultaneously. Excessive max strength / max speed development is explicitly de-emphasized; power-endurance and strength-endurance are the primary targets. Operator context: relative strength + aerobic capacity + mental durability. Programs are 1-month blocks, repeatable 2–3× or cycled between Operator I / Operator II.

archetype.name: Gym Jones Operator Strength (SL Squat / Step-Up / FLR)
archetype.notes: Gym Jones Operator Fitness I and II primary strength session structure. Opens with a wall squat mobility drill, then progresses to the unilateral strength block: single-leg squat (box) or weighted step-up. The session closes with the Front Leaning Rest (FLR) on rings — 300 accumulated seconds of ring support hold as a shoulder and core endurance block. Principle: relative strength over absolute strength. No bilateral barbell work in this template — all primary loading is unilateral.

slots.notes: Wall squat mobility drill. 3×5 before any lower body session.
Unilateral squat strength. Single-leg squat (box) 5×5 each side. Progress by lowering box height toward pistol range. If box pistols are mastered, advance to weighted step-up.
Weighted step-up 5×2 each side at heavy load (work up to 95–135 lb barbell or equivalent DB). Rest 60 sec between sets. Eliminate all trailing-leg assistance.
FLR (Front Leaning Rest) on rings — 300 accumulated seconds. 5×60 sec ring support hold, rings turned out. Rest as needed between sets. If rings are unavailable, substitute plank hold on floor.

deload.notes: Reduce to 3×3 on the strength block. Hold FLR for 3×30 sec. Keep mobility drill unchanged.

time_limited.notes: Drop loaded step-up if time < 40 min. Prioritize mobility + primary unilateral strength + FLR.

substitutions.substitute_approach: Substitute plank hold (floor or push-up position) for ring support hold.

exercise.name: Wall Squat (Mobility Drill)
exercise.notes: Gym Jones warm-up staple used in virtually every strength and circuit session. Stand with toes touching a wall, feet wide. Drop into a squat with knees tracking toes; contact the wall with knees to enforce vertical shin position and upright torso. Hands brace against wall as needed. Builds ankle mobility, hip flexor opening, and thoracic extension. Not a strength exercise — a diagnostic and mobility drill. 2–3 sets of 5 before any lower body session.

exercises.notes: Wall squat mobility drill. 3×5 before any lower body session.

exercise.notes: CrossFit fundamental movement. Rippetoe squatting standards apply: below parallel, neutral spine, heels flat. Gym Jones warm-up protocol: 2×5 wall squats then 2×10 air squats before loading. Chelsea benchmark: 15 squats per minute EMOM 30 min.

exercises.notes: Unilateral squat strength. Single-leg squat (box) 5×5 each side. Progress by lowering box height toward pistol range. If box pistols are mastered, advance to weighted step-up.

archetype.name: Gym Jones TGU Recovery (100 Total Reps)
archetype.notes: Gym Jones recovery session: 100 total Turkish Get-Up reps at a sub-maximal load (typically 16 kg for advanced athletes; 12 kg for intermediate). Performed at a slow, deliberate pace — this is restorative, not conditioning. Each rep demands full shoulder stability, hip flexor mobility, and joint integrity through a complex multi-position movement. The high rep count at low load flushes the tissues without adding stress load. Twight on TGU recovery: "Movement quality under fatigue. The fatigue reveals the compensation patterns." Take all the rest you need — the goal is 100 quality reps, not speed.

slots.notes: 10×5 TGU alternating sides (or 10×10 if counting per arm). Use a light bell — this is recovery, not strength. Rest 60–90 sec between sets. Focus on positional quality at each pause point: floor press, half-kneeling, standing. Reach 100 total reps.

deload.notes: Reduce to 60 total reps (6×5 sets). Drop load by one KB size.

time_limited.notes: Reduce total reps to 50 (5×5) if session time < 40 min. Maintain movement quality over volume.

substitutions.substitute_approach: A dumbbell can substitute for TGU. Grip is different but the movement pattern is preserved.

archetype.name: Barbell Power Complex (Olympic Lift Derivatives)
sources: Starting Strength — power clean as supplemental lift
archetype.notes: Barbell power development session built around Olympic lift derivatives: power clean, hang power clean, push press, and pull. These movements develop rate of force development and neuromuscular power in a way that carries over to athletic performance and GPP. Gym Jones uses power cleans as an integral part of strength training — not for competition but for the athletic quality they develop. Load is submaximal; bar speed is the quality metric. Technique prerequisite: athletes must be competent at the hip hinge pattern before performing power cleans. At novice level, default to KB ballistic session instead. Intermediate+ athletes are cleared for barbell power work. Rest fully between power sets (3-4 min) — power drops immediately when fatigue accumulates. Do not rush warm-up sets.

slots.notes: 5-min targeted prep: thoracic rotation, ankle dorsiflexion, and hip hinge with dowel. Power clean requires full thoracic extension and rack position (front squat depth). Check wrist mobility for rack position.

5 × 3 power clean or hang power clean at 70-80% of power clean max. Bar speed is the priority metric — if bar speed slows, stop the set. Selector upgrades novice athletes (hang power clean) to power clean as they accumulate sessions. Reset to the floor each rep; do not touch-and-go — this is a power session, not conditioning.

Push press 4 × 5 at working weight. Push press (leg drive) is preferred over strict press for a power session — the leg drive trains rate of force development through the kinetic chain. Load: the bar should move explosively. If you cannot use leg drive to initiate bar movement, reduce load.
Romanian deadlift or conventional deadlift 3 × 8 at moderate load. Posterior chain reinforcement — not the primary focus of this session, so load is sub-maximal. Controlled eccentric (3 sec down).

deload.notes: Reduce power clean to 3 × 2. Drop push press to 3 × 4 at 75%. Drop posterior chain accessory. Maintain bar speed as primary metric even at deload loads.

time_limited.notes: Drop the accessory work. Primary + overhead press are the stimulus.

substitutions.substitute_approach: Replace with KB ballistic session (swings, cleans, snatches). KB ballistics train the same hip-drive power quality without a barbell. Use the heaviest available bell for swing/clean work.

archetype.name: Gym Jones Accumulation Circuit (Goblet Squat / Bear Crawl / Carry)
archetype.notes: Gym Jones accumulation-style circuit combining a high-rep squat movement, locomotion, and a loaded carry. Emphasis on total volume and time under load rather than maximal intensity. Used as a GPP conditioning day between heavier strength sessions. Movements cycle through lower push, locomotion, and carry patterns. Rest is minimal between movements; take 2–3 min between rounds. Target: 3–5 rounds depending on fitness level.

slots.notes: 8-min easy movement prep. Light jogging or dynamic mobility.
High-rep goblet squat with a moderate KB (16–24 kg). 3×20. Accumulate squat volume — this is endurance, not max strength.
Bear crawl 3×20 m. Minimal rest between lengths. Builds shoulder stability and hip flexor endurance.
Farmer carry 3×40 m. Use heavy KBs or DBs — challenging but completable. Grip endurance is the limiting factor. Alternate farmer, rack, and overhead carry week to week for variety.

deload.notes: Reduce to 2 rounds. Drop squat reps to 10. Reduce carry distance to 20 m.

time_limited.notes: Drop carry if session time < 35 min. Prioritize squat volume and locomotion block.

substitutions.substitute_approach: Substitute dumbbell goblet squat. Use dumbbells for farmer carry. All movements can be performed with DB.

archetype.name: Gym Jones Aerobic Recovery (Row / Swim / Ruck)
archetype.notes: Gym Jones recovery-day format: 60-120 min of easy, continuous, low-impact work at conversational pace. The purpose is circulation and aerobic development between hard sessions, not additional stress — Twight's rule is that the recovery day must actually recover, and an athlete who turns it into a third hard session loses the following week. Row is the default (Concept II is the house ergometer); swim and ruck are equally valid. Damper 4-6, 18-22 SPM.

slots.notes: 60 min continuous, Zone 1-2. Conversational throughout: if you cannot hold a sentence, you are working too hard and this has stopped being a recovery session. Duration scales to the athlete's budget; intensity never does.
10 min of unloaded hip, thoracic and shoulder work while warm.

deload.notes: 35-40 min. Already a low-stress session; shorten rather than soften.

time_limited.notes: Keep the aerobic work. Under 30 min the session still has value — unlike the hard sessions, this one does not need a minimum dose to be worth doing.

substitutions.substitute_approach: Swim, ruck at 15-20 kg, or bike. Low-impact is the priority since this session sits between hard days.

goal.name: Horsemen GPP / SOF-Style Training

track.name: 4-Month Macro
track.description: The source's four months — strength, power endurance, job specific, maintenance — each a 28-day template started on the 1st of the month, with the days left over free, and the whole run two or three times. Every week is six training days and a rest day. The strength and conditioning numbers the source names are what it aims to reach in four months.

phase_sequence.name: Strength
phase_sequence.description: Month one: strength twice a week, on days 1 and 5; a job-specific day, a power-endurance day and one rotating day (SMMF, power, a progression workout or a circuit) between them; recovery on day 6 and rest on day 7. Strength days work up to a 1RM in the day's lift, then percentages of it, then accessory rounds; there is no RPE. The source lists the PT test among its hard job-specific options and never schedules it; here it takes the month's first hard job-specific day (week 2) as a baseline for the four-month goals.
adaptations: Maximal strength toward the bodyweight goals
Power endurance and job-specific capacity kept alongside it
phase_sequence.intensity: Heavy: a 1RM worked up to on the day, then percentages of it

phase_sequence.name: Power Endurance
phase_sequence.description: Month two puts power endurance first — about four sessions every two weeks: runs with get-ups, the Secret Service Snatch Test, Tabata, a 5K row, EMOMs. Strength drops to maintenance, about twice in two weeks, beside job-specific days, an endurance session of 60 minutes or more, recovery and a rest day each week.

phase_sequence.name: Job Specific
phase_sequence.description: Month three makes job-specific days most of the week: climbing and grip work, leg blasters, a ruck run, the PT tests, tire and sled work. Strength and power endurance alternate around them, with recovery on day 6 and rest on day 7.

phase_sequence.name: Maintenance
phase_sequence.description: Month four holds what the macro built: recovery twice a week at 65% of max heart rate or less, circuits, strength, and a hard job-specific day, with rest on day 7. The PT test, one of the source's hard job-specific options, takes the macro's last hard job-specific day: the most rested point of the four months, and the check against their goals.
phase_sequence.intensity: Hard days between recovery at ≤65% max HR

goal.notes: Written by "the Horsemen" for special-operations operators ("Team guys") to build a broad operator base of fitness. It states no prerequisites and has no novice path; daily 1RM work, Olympic lifts at 80-100% and gymnastics such as handstand push-ups and rope climbs assume an experienced athlete. Its numbers are goals to reach within four months, not entry standards: deadlift 2.5x, front squat 1.5x, bench press 1.5x and military press 1.0x bodyweight, 3 miles in under 20:00, and at least 200 on the Secret Service Snatch Test (SSST). The PT test is a separate list: max pull-ups (minimum 15), sit-ups in 3 minutes (90), push-ups in 3 minutes (80), a 3-mile run (22:30) and an 800 m swim (14:30). The program is four 28-day months — strength, power endurance, job specific, maintenance — run two or three times. Every week is six sessions and a rest day, with recovery days (30-60 minutes at 65% of max heart rate or less) built in. Each day is a category — strength, power endurance, job specific, SMMF, progression, circuits, density, accumulation, endurance or recovery — and the workout is picked from that category's list of named workouts. Loads come from a 1RM worked up to on the day, then percentages of it, fixed loads or multiples of bodyweight; there is no RPE and no deload week. The 4-Month Macro track runs the source as written: each month's week templates day by day, every named workout as an archetype in its category's pool, taken in rotation, and prescribed exactly as the source writes it (src/week_template.py). A workout whose equipment the athlete lacks is passed over for the next one; names carrying profanity or a slur are cleaned.

goal.name: Mark Wildman Kettlebell

track.name: General Practice
track.description: Wildman's Phase II programs on the Tetris of Training — swing, clean and press, Turkish get-up, deck squat and, once confirmed, snatch — each twice a week on nonconsecutive days, as many as the week's time holds. Each runs its Nerd Math cycle at one bell and starts again with a heavier one; progress is per clean session, never by the calendar.

phase_sequence.name: Build
phase_sequence.focus: Repeat the fundamentals; cycle each program, then a heavier bell
phase_sequence.description: The swing runs the Nerd Math program's four approaches: 6 to 20 swings a minute over 10 minutes, then over 20, then start/stop swings in ten and twenty 90-second rounds — sixteen weeks at two sessions a week. Clean and press, get-up and deck squat run their own cycles beside it, as the session time allows; the snatch joins after clean and press once it is confirmed. A cycle finished cleanly is repeated with a heavier bell. Wildman calls Phase II the one you are never done with.
adaptations: Repeated skill practice at a stable bell
Density, then volume, then a heavier bell
phase_sequence.intensity: Clean mechanics, RPE 7 or below; rest within every minute

exercise.name: Kettlebell Turkish Get-Up
exercise.notes: From lying to standing with bell locked overhead throughout; reverse to return. Foundational Wildman movement — practiced in nearly every session. Gym Jones: 100 TGUs at 15 lb (recovery) and 5–6 reps at 25 lb (strength). Horsemen SMMF: 100 get-ups at 35 lb (15–20 min). Tests shoulder stability, hip mobility, and whole-body integration. Wildman: move slowly through every position; there are no shortcuts.
